role.q: What does a Product Owner do, and how is it different from a project manager?
role.why: The opening question of most PO interviews: it checks that you see the role as owning value, not managing tasks.
role.model: A Product Owner is accountable for the value of the product: they set the product goal, own and order the backlog, and decide what the team builds next, based on users, data and the business. A project manager is accountable for delivering an agreed scope on time and on budget, and coordinates people and plans. In Scrum the PO does not assign work or manage the team: the developers decide how to build it. In practice the PO spends a lot of time with users and stakeholders, writes and refines items with the team, accepts what is done, and checks after release whether it changed the metric it was meant to change.

role.q: How do you prioritise the backlog when everyone says their request is urgent?
role.why: The question PO interviews never skip: they want a method and the courage to say no.
role.model: I make the criteria visible instead of arguing request by request. I tie each item to the product goal and score it with a simple method, for example RICE (reach, impact, confidence, effort) or MoSCoW for a release, and I share the scores. Urgent requests get the same treatment, plus a question: what happens if we do it in two sprints instead of now? When two stakeholders disagree, I bring them together with the data, and if it is still a tie the sponsor decides; I write the decision down. Saying no is easier when the backlog shows what would be delayed.

role.q: Write a user story for a feature of your choice, with its acceptance criteria.
role.why: A practical test of the most common PO deliverable: is the story about a user need, small enough, and testable?
role.model: Example for a job site: As a job seeker who works during the day, I want to get new offers for my saved search by e-mail every morning, so that I can apply before other candidates. Acceptance criteria: Given I am signed in and have a saved search, when I turn on the alert, then I receive at most one e-mail a day with only the offers I have not seen yet. Given there are no new offers, then no e-mail is sent. Given I click unsubscribe in the e-mail, then the alert is turned off. It is small enough for one sprint, it says who and why, and each criterion can be tested.

role.q: How do you know a feature was a success?
role.why: Recruiters want POs who measure outcomes, not output: shipping is not the goal.
role.model: I define success before we build: one main metric tied to the user problem, for example the share of new users who finish onboarding, plus a guardrail metric such as support tickets. I check the baseline, agree on the target with the team, and look at the data one or two weeks after release, through the analytics tool or a SQL query. When it is possible, I release to part of the users first or run an A/B test. If the metric did not move, we look at why with user feedback and decide to iterate, change approach or remove the feature, and we say so in the sprint review.

role.q: How do you run product discovery before building something?
role.why: It shows whether you reduce risk before spending the team’s time, or only write requirements.
role.model: I start from a problem, not a solution: what users are trying to do and where it hurts. I talk to five to eight users with open questions about what they did last time, not what they would like, and I look at the data and support tickets. Then I write the main assumptions and test the riskiest one cheaply: a mock-up in Figma, a fake door, a prototype. Only when the problem and the direction are confirmed do I write stories for delivery. Discovery and delivery run in parallel: the team builds what was validated while I explore the next problem.

role.q: A stakeholder wants a feature added in the middle of a sprint. What do you do?
role.why: It tests your knowledge of Scrum and how you protect the team while staying helpful.
role.model: First I understand the request and the real deadline. In Scrum the sprint goal is protected: I do not push work into the sprint without the developers, and most requests can wait for the next sprint planning, which I explain with the date. If it is truly critical, for example a legal deadline or a production problem, I talk with the team: they decide whether it fits, and if something has to come out, we agree on what. If the new work makes the sprint goal obsolete, the PO can cancel the sprint, but that is rare. Either way I tell the stakeholder clearly what will happen and when.

role.q: Tell me about a time you said no to a stakeholder.
role.why: A behavioural question: they want a real example, told in STAR form, where you kept the relationship.
role.model: Situation: during my studies project, the sales lead asked for a custom export for one client. Task: as the person ordering the backlog, I had to decide. Action: I asked what problem the client had, found that two other clients had asked for the same data, and proposed a standard export in the next release instead of a one-off, with the data showing what the one-off would have delayed. Result: the sales lead agreed, the standard export served three clients, and the planned feature shipped on time. What I learned: a no goes down better with the reason, an alternative and a date.

role.q: What is in your product roadmap, and how often does it change?
role.why: It checks that you see a roadmap as a communication tool about outcomes, not a list of promised features.
role.model: My roadmap is organised by outcomes and problems, with a short horizon in detail and a longer one in themes: Now, Next, Later. Each item says what we want to change and how we will measure it, not only the feature. It changes when we learn something: results of a release, new user research, a change in strategy. I review it at least every quarter with stakeholders and update it after each sprint review if needed. I avoid fixed dates far ahead; when a date matters, for example a contract, I say how confident we are.
